(Entertainment Weekly) -- It was a glass half-full, glass half-empty kind of weekend at the box office for "Funny People," writer-director Judd Apatow's comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death. Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen star in "Funny People," which took the No. 1 slot at the box office this weekend. According to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office, it opened at the top spot with an estimated $23.4 million, better than Apatow's The 40 Year-Old Virgin ($21.4 million) -- hence, the glass is half full. But that figure is far lower than the debut for Apatow's "Knocked Up" ($30.7 million), and it's the worst opening for a comedy for star Adam Sander since his 2000 turkey "Little Nicky" -- hence, the glass is half empty. Of course, "Funny People" was billed more as a thoughtful dramedy than a balls-out Sandler laugh-fest, and when matched against the opening frames for Sandler's serious efforts "Reign Over Me," "Spanglish," and "Punch-Drunk Love," Funny People is far and away the winner -- and the glass is half full again. But whether it's a comedy, drama, or dramedy, "Funny People's" $75 million budget is quite the handful of pretty pennies, and with a shaky "B-" Cinemascore, the film is going to have a hard time overcoming tepid word-of-mouth -- and we're back to the half-empty glass. So let's just move on, shall we? The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, definitely runneth over. Thanks to its debut on IMAX (and the premium ticket prices that come with it), "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" came in second with $17.7 million, a soft 40 percent drop from last weekend for $255.5 million total. At this rate, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the 'Potter' franchise. The guinea pigs of "G-Force" were right on its heels at third place, nibbling up $17.1 million, a decent 46 percent drop for a two-week cume of $66.5 million. And Katherine Heigl's romcom "The Ugly Truth" took in an additional $13 million, a 53 percent drop for fourth place and $54.5 million total. Of the two other wide releases this weekend, at least the sci-fi family comedy "Aliens in the Attic" -- which grossed a meager $7.8 million for fifth place -- broke into the top 10. The torture porn flick "The Collector" collected a grisly $3.6 million and plopped dead at 11th place. Box office on a whole was down a massive 22 percent from last year, when The "Dark Knight" and "The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor" both took in over $40 million, but the specialty market showed some vibrant signs of life. Bone fide indie hit "(500) Days of Summer" expanded to 266 theaters for $2.7 million, a $10,338 per theater average. And three widely disparate films opened in four theaters each to healthy per theater averages: The quirky romantic comedy "Adam" ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film "Thirst" ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary "The Cove" ($13,600 per theater). Finally, a true milestone was reached this weekend by "The Hangover." With $5.1 million this weekend for a running total of $255.8 million, the summer's biggest die hard blockbuster has passed "Star Trek" and (for a brief moment) "Harry Potter 6" as the third highest grossing movie of the year. # Weekly Entertainment: Your Dose of Fun and Laughter

Everyone needs a little entertainment to break up the routine of daily life, and what better way to unwind than with a weekly dose of funny content? Whether you're catching up on your favorite comedy shows, scrolling through hilarious memes, or watching viral videos, entertainment plays a vital role in keeping our spirits high.

## Why Weekly Entertainment Matters

Setting aside time each week for entertainment isn't just about killing time—it's about recharging your mind and lifting your mood. Laughter has been proven to reduce stress, boost your immune system, and even strengthen relationships. A good laugh with friends over a funny sitcom or a comedy special can turn an ordinary evening into a memorable one.

## The Power of Funny Content

Humor is universal. From stand-up comedy and sketch shows to funny podcasts and comedic movies, there's something out there for every sense of humor. The best part about funny entertainment is how it brings people together. Sharing a joke, quoting a hilarious scene, or laughing at an unexpected moment creates connections that last.

## Making It a Weekly Habit

Consider carving out a specific time each week dedicated to entertainment. Here are a few ideas:

- **Comedy Night:** Pick a funny movie or comedy special to enjoy.
- **Meme Monday:** Start your week by sharing the funniest posts with friends.
- **Podcast Fridays:** Wind down with a comedy podcast that keeps you laughing.

## Final Thoughts

Entertainment, especially the funny kind, is more than just a way to pass the time. It's a weekly tradition worth embracing—one that keeps you smiling, connected, and ready to take on whatever comes next. So go ahead, find something funny this week, and let the laughter roll!

# Weekend Box Office: Adam Sandler's 'Funny People' Tops Chart Despite Soft Opening

**By Entertainment Weekly Staff**

Adam Sandler and Judd Apatow's dramedy *Funny People* claimed the No. 1 spot this weekend, but the R-rated collaboration landed with less of a punchline than Universal had hoped, opening to an estimated $23.4 million.

## The Top Five

The Universal release, which reunites Sandler with his former roommate Apatow for the writer-director's third feature, marked a soft debut for a movie carrying a hefty price tag and an all-star comedic pedigree. The film, which co-stars Seth Rogen, Leslie Mann, and Eric Bana, drew an older-skewing crowd, with audiences responding tepidly to its two-and-a-half-hour runtime and its darker meditation on mortality and celebrity.

Holding strong in second place was Disney/Pixar's *G-Force*, the 3-D talking-guinea-pig adventure, which added roughly $17.1 million in its second weekend for a running domestic total in the neighborhood of $66 million.

*The Ugly Truth*, Sony's Katherine Heigl–Gerard Butler romantic comedy, settled into third with about $13 million, showing solid legs after its own No. 1 debut the previous frame.

Rounding out the top five were the Harry Potter franchise's *Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince*, still conjuring strong numbers well into its run, and the raunchy comedy *The Hangover*, Warner Bros.' summer sleeper that continued its remarkable staying power on its march past the $260 million mark.

## Budget Concerns

The bigger story of the weekend was whether *Funny People* could justify its reported production budget of roughly $75 million—steep for a comedy—plus tens of millions more in marketing. Apatow's previous directorial efforts, *The 40-Year-Old Virgin* and *Knocked Up*, were made for far less and became breakout hits. *Funny People*'s more expensive, more ambitious swing puts pressure on strong word-of-mouth and international grosses to reach profitability.

## Indie and Limited Releases

On the specialty front, the weekend offered a mixed bag. Several limited platform releases jockeyed for arthouse attention, with distributors betting on strong per-theater averages to build momentum through the late-summer season. The indie sector continued to serve as counterprogramming for adult audiences seeking alternatives to the multiplex's tentpole offerings.

## Year-Over-Year

Overall, the marketplace continued its impressive 2009 pace, with the summer box office running comfortably ahead of the same period last year. Buoyed by a steady stream of hits throughout the season, Hollywood remained on track to post record-setting grosses—welcome news during an otherwise challenging economic climate, and a reminder of the enduring appeal of moviegoing as affordable escapism.

Check back next weekend as *G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra* storms into theaters, looking to blow the competition out of the water.

*(Note: All figures are estimates and should be verified against final studio reports.)*

# 'Funny People' Opens to Modest $22.7 Million, Failing to Match Apatow's Comedy Pedigree

Judd Apatow's dramatic comedy "Funny People" landed in the No. 1 spot at the box office this weekend, but the ambitious Adam Sandler vehicle fell well short of the blockbuster expectations that typically accompany a film from the reigning king of R-rated comedy.

The Universal release grossed an estimated $22.7 million from 3,008 theaters, translating to a lukewarm per-screen average of roughly $7,547. While claiming the top position is nothing to sneeze at, the number represents a significant step down from Apatow's previous directorial efforts—and raises questions about whether audiences were ready to embrace the filmmaker's darker, more introspective side.

## A Departure from the Apatow Formula

To understand why "Funny People" underperformed relative to expectations, it helps to look at how Apatow's earlier films launched. "Knocked Up" opened to a robust $30.7 million in June 2007 before going on to gross more than $148 million domestically. His directorial debut, "The 40-Year-Old Virgin," bowed to a solid $21.4 million in 2005 and legged out to $109 million thanks to strong word of mouth.

At first glance, "Funny People" actually edged out "Virgin's" opening figure. But context matters: ticket prices have climbed considerably in the intervening years, and "Funny People" carried a reported production budget in the neighborhood of $75 million—dwarfing the modest costs of Apatow's earlier, breezier comedies. This is a film that needed to open big, and it didn't.

## The Sandler Factor

The results are perhaps most surprising when measured against Adam Sandler's own track record. The comedy superstar has reliably opened films north of $30 and $40 million throughout his career. "I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry" debuted to $34.2 million, while "You Don't Mess with the Zohan" launched with $38.5 million just last year. Even "Bedtime Stories," his family-friendly Disney outing, opened strong.

"Funny People" asked Sandler to play a variation on himself—a wildly successful but spiritually hollow comedian named George Simmons who receives a terminal diagnosis. The meta, melancholy premise, combined with a lengthy 146-minute runtime and a hard R rating, likely narrowed the film's commercial appeal. Audiences accustomed to Sandler's broad, good-natured comedies may have been caught off guard by the movie's tonal ambitions and its unflinching examination of mortality and regret.

## What the Numbers Say

Exit polling suggested a somewhat divided audience response, with the film earning a modest "B" CinemaScore—not the kind of enthusiastic grade that signals the strong word of mouth Apatow's previous films enjoyed. The crowd skewed older and male, which limited the picture's four-quadrant potential.

The lengthy runtime also worked against the film logistically, reducing the number of daily showtimes theaters could program compared to a standard 95-minute comedy.

## The Competition

Holding strong in the No. 2 position was "G-Force," Disney's 3-D talking-guinea-pig adventure, which added an estimated $17.1 million in its second weekend for a 44 percent drop and a healthy domestic total. Rounding out the top five were holdovers including "The Ugly Truth," "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince," and "Orphan," each continuing to draw steady summer crowds.

## The Bottom Line

While "Funny People" claimed the weekend crown, its opening serves as a reminder that even the most bankable names in comedy face limits when they venture into more challenging territory. Apatow deserves credit for his creative ambition, and the film's ultimate financial fate will hinge on whether adult audiences continue seeking it out in the weeks ahead. But for a movie assembled from this much comedic firepower—Apatow, Sandler, Seth Rogen, and a murderer's row of supporting players—a $22.7 million debut can only be judged a disappointment.

The real test comes next weekend, when the film will need to demonstrate the kind of staying power that turned Apatow's earlier hits into genuine phenomena. If the drop-off is steep, "Funny People" may go down as the rare Apatow-Sandler collaboration that couldn't quite find its audience.

*Check back next weekend for the latest box office results.*

# Weekend Box Office Analysis: Comedy Stumbles as Family Fare and Wizardry Endure

**July 31 – August 2, 2009**

The final weekend of July delivered a mixed bag of results, headlined by a high-profile comedy that failed to fully capitalize on its star power, while holdovers demonstrated remarkable staying power and a scrappy indie continued its impressive expansion.

## Judd Apatow's Ambitious Gamble Comes Up Short

Universal's **"Funny People"** claimed the top spot, but the victory carried an asterisk. The Judd Apatow-directed dramedy, starring Adam Sandler as a comedian confronting his mortality alongside Seth Rogen, opened to roughly **$22.7 million**—a soft number for a film pairing one of comedy's most bankable stars with the director behind "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" and "Knocked Up."

The disappointing debut likely stems from several factors. At nearly two and a half hours, the film's runtime is unusually long for the genre, and its darker, more introspective tone diverged from the broad comedy audiences may have expected from a Sandler vehicle. Marketing that emphasized laughs may have set up a mismatch with the more melancholy final product. With a reported budget in the $75 million range, the film faces an uphill climb toward profitability.

## "G-Force" Holds Firm with Family Audiences

Disney's 3D spy-guinea-pig adventure **"G-Force"** proved the durability of family entertainment during the summer stretch, landing in second place with approximately **$17 million** in its second weekend—a modest decline that pushed its domestic total past the **$66 million** mark. The Jerry Bruckheimer production continues to benefit from premium 3D ticket pricing and a lack of direct competition for younger viewers.

## Potter's Enduring Magic

In its third weekend, **"Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince"** refused to relinquish its grip on audiences, adding roughly **$13.9 million** and driving its domestic cumulative total toward **$258 million**. Warner Bros.' sixth installment in the franchise continues to demonstrate the extraordinary reliability of the boy wizard, tracking as one of the year's biggest performers both domestically and internationally.

## The Rest of the Field

Rounding out the top tier, **"The Ugly Truth"** (Sony) held reasonably well in its second frame with around **$13 million**, buoyed by the star chemistry of Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler. Meanwhile, Fox's **"Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs"** and Paramount's still-formidable **"Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen"** continued their long tails deep into the summer season.

## Specialty Spotlight: Summer Belongs to "(500) Days"

The weekend's most encouraging story unfolded in the specialty market, where Fox Searchlight's **"(500) Days of Summer"** continued a stellar rollout. The unconventional romance starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel expanded its theater count aggressively while maintaining strong per-screen averages—the hallmark of genuine word-of-mouth momentum.

Marc Webb's directorial debut, with its nonlinear structure and refreshingly honest take on modern relationships, has emerged as counter-programming catnip for adult audiences seeking an alternative to the summer's tentpole spectacle. Its trajectory suggests a long, profitable platform run ahead.

## The Takeaway

This weekend underscored a persistent summer truth: star power alone no longer guarantees blockbuster openings, particularly when a film's tone and length work against commercial expectations. While "Funny People" will test the theory that Apatow's brand can weather a slow start through strong word-of-mouth, the real winners were the reliable family and franchise offerings—and a small-budget indie proving that a great story still travels far.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Weekend at the Movies: Half-Empty, Half-Full, All Adam Sandler

There are two ways to look at the box office performance of Judd Apatow's *Funny People* this weekend, and both of them are correct—which is precisely the problem.

**Glass Half-Full:** Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen delivered the number-one movie in America, opening to a respectable haul that no other film could touch. For a two-and-a-half-hour dramedy about a comedian dying of a mysterious blood disease—not exactly the elevator pitch that screams "summer blockbuster"—landing at the top of the heap is nothing to sneeze at. Apatow got to make his ambitious, personal passion project, and audiences showed up to buy tickets.

**Glass Half-Empty:** They just didn't buy *enough* of them. When you slap Sandler and Rogen on the marquee and spend a reported nine-figure budget getting butts in seats, "number one with a modest opening" starts to feel like a participation trophy. Universal was surely hoping for *Knocked Up* numbers; instead they got a film that reminds you comedies about death are a hard sell in July, when audiences would rather laugh without contemplating their own mortality.

The truth, as always, lives in the murky middle. *Funny People* is the rare movie that's simultaneously a winner and a disappointment—a glass that's technically full to the halfway mark, which is another way of saying it's also empty to the halfway mark.

## The Rest of the Field

Holding strong in the rearview mirror, **G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra** continued to prove that critic-proof is a real phenomenon, drawing crowds who wanted explosions without existential dread. Meanwhile, **Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince** kept working its box-office magic several weekends into its run, siphoning off ticket buyers with the reliability of a well-cast spell.

**The Ugly Truth**, the Katherine Heigl–Gerard Butler rom-com, continued to charm its way through the counter-programming lane, offering the light romantic escapism that *Funny People* pointedly refused to.

## On the Art-House Circuit

In limited release, the specialty crowd had plenty to chew on. Smaller films continued platforming in select cities, banking on strong per-screen averages and word-of-mouth to build momentum—the tortoise strategy in a summer built for hares.

**The Takeaway:** In a weekend defined by mixed signals, *Funny People* captured the mood perfectly. It's a hit and a miss, a triumph and a shrug. Half-full, half-empty—and, either way, half as funny as its title promised.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an entertainment journalism piece reporting on how "The Hangover" became the third highest grossing movie of the year, set within a full recap of the summer 2009 weekend box office.
counterfactuals.output:
# Summer 2009's Wildest Underdog: How "The Hangover" Partied Its Way to Box Office Glory

*An entertainment journalism retrospective*

---

When Warner Bros. slotted a raunchy, R-rated comedy about a bachelor party gone catastrophically wrong into the crowded summer of 2009, few industry watchers expected it to become one of the defining stories of the season. Yet "The Hangover" didn't just survive a summer stacked with franchise heavyweights and special-effects spectacles—it thrived, ultimately clawing its way to become the **third highest-grossing film of the year**, an almost unthinkable feat for a comedy with no established stars headlining above the title.

## A Deceptively Quiet Opening

"The Hangover" debuted the weekend of June 5, 2009, and while its opening was strong, it wasn't the kind of number that screamed "phenomenon." It landed atop the weekend with a solid but not earth-shattering figure, edging out a well-marketed animated release. The bigger story, at least in the moment, seemed to be whether Todd Phillips' comedy had staying power against the relentless summer pipeline.

That question was answered emphatically over the following weeks.

## The Legs That Defied Gravity

What separated "The Hangover" from its peers was its extraordinary word-of-mouth. In an era when most films front-load their grosses and shed 50-60% of their audience in the second weekend, Phillips' comedy pulled off something remarkable: it barely dropped. Audiences weren't just seeing it—they were *returning*, dragging friends along to experience the misadventures of Phil, Stu, Alan, and their search for a missing groom through the wreckage of Las Vegas.

Week after week, "The Hangover" held its ground while blockbusters around it collapsed under their own weight. It became the film people talked about at the office, the sleeper that turned Zach Galifianakis into an overnight sensation and cemented the "wolfpack" into the cultural lexicon.

## The Summer It Had to Beat

The comedy's climb is all the more impressive when measured against the competition it outlasted.

**"Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen"** dominated its late-June opening with the kind of explosive numbers only Michael Bay and a Hasbro property can generate, ultimately ranking among the year's absolute top earners. **"Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince"** arrived in mid-July as a franchise juggernaut, commanding the box office with the loyalty of a global fan base. Pixar's **"Up"** floated in just before "The Hangover," charming critics and families alike into a lucrative, sustained run.

Add to that the summer arrivals of **"Star Trek,"** J.J. Abrams' franchise revival that earned critical raves; **"Terminator Salvation"**; **"Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian"**; and the animated **"Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs,"** and you have a season absolutely packed with tentpoles engineered for box-office supremacy.

## The Weekend Rhythm of a Crowded Season

The summer 2009 box office played out like a weekly heavyweight bout. Each Friday brought a new challenger to the top of the charts, and the leaderboard reshuffled constantly:

- Animated hits and family films traded the top spot with action spectacles
- Franchise sequels muscled in for their opening weekends before receding
- Counter-programming dramas and thrillers carved out their niches

Through all of it, "The Hangover" refused to disappear. While flashier films burned bright and faded, the comedy remained a fixture in the top ten for an astonishingly long stretch, quietly accumulating a fortune one strong weekend at a time.

## The Final Tally

When the dust settled on the year, the math told a stunning story. "The Hangover" had out-grossed nearly every film released in 2009 domestically, trailing only the year's two biggest titans to claim the **number three spot**. For an R-rated comedy—a genre often relegated to modest expectations—to finish ahead of star-studded dramas, animated tentpoles, and expensive action franchises was nothing short of a coup.

## The Legacy

The film's success rewrote conventional wisdom about what a comedy could achieve in a summer built for spectacle. It launched a franchise, minted new comedy stars, and proved that a sharp premise executed with fearless commitment could go toe-to-toe with the biggest budgets Hollywood had to offer.

In a season defined by robots, wizards, and starships, the last laugh belonged to a group of hungover friends stumbling through Las Vegas—and it turned out to be one of the most profitable laughs of the entire year.
